item.question: A circle is drawn with its centre marked, and some points are marked on the circle. Use the points on the circle and/or the centre to form isosceles triangles.
steps_tex: Mark the centre $O$ and two points $P$ and $Q$ on the circle. Join $OP$, $OQ$ and $PQ$.
$OP$ and $OQ$ are both radii of the same circle, so $OP = OQ$ and triangle $OPQ$ is isosceles.
Choosing $P$ and $Q$ so that $PQ$ is also equal to the radius makes all three sides equal: an equilateral triangle.
Three points on the circle can also give an isosceles triangle: take $P$ and $Q$, then take $R$ halfway between them on the circle, so that $RP = RQ$.
item.answer_tex: Any two points on the circle with the centre give an isosceles triangle; two points whose distance is one radius give an equilateral triangle

Three circles: $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the centres and every pair of centres is one radius apart, so triangle $ABC$ is equilateral. Each pair of circles crosses in two points, and each crossing point together with those two centres gives another equilateral triangle.
Any point on a circle with the centre and another point on the same circle gives an isosceles triangle, as in the single circle.

item.question: A tent, a tree and a pole are the three corners of a plot. The tent to the tree is 30 m in a straight line, the tent to the pole is 20 m and the pole to the tree is 25 m. Which way is shorter?
steps: Direct path from the tent to the tree: 30 m.
Roundabout path from the tent to the pole and then to the tree: 20 m + 25 m = 45 m.
30 m is less than 45 m, so the direct path is shorter.
The same holds for every pair of the three corners: each direct path is shorter than the roundabout path through the third corner.
item.answer: The direct path of 30 m is shorter than the roundabout path of 45 m

item.question: Try to construct a triangle with sidelengths 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm, then 2 cm, 3 cm and 6 cm, and say what happens to the arcs.
steps_tex: Take $8\text{ cm}$ as the base $AB$. Draw an arc of $3\text{ cm}$ from $A$ and an arc of $4\text{ cm}$ from $B$.
From $A$, the arc reaches $3\text{ cm}$ along the base and the arc from $B$ reaches $4\text{ cm}$ back, which covers $3 + 4 = 7\text{ cm}$ of the $8\text{ cm}$. They do not meet.

item.question: A triangle has two sides of 6 cm and 5 cm that meet at a corner, and the angle at that corner is 30°. Is 30° the included angle? What if the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side?
steps: The two given sides, 6 cm and 5 cm, meet at one corner. The angle at that corner is between them, so 30° is the included angle.
If the 30° angle were at the other end of the 6 cm side, one of its arms would be the 6 cm side but the other arm would be a side that is not given.
That angle is not between the two given sides, so it is not the included angle. The measurements would then be a different kind of data.
item.answer: Yes, 30° is included when it sits between the 6 cm and 5 cm sides; at the other end it is not

item.question: Say why no triangle can be built from the angles 90°, 5 cm, 90°, and from 100°, 5 cm, 95°.
steps: Draw the base of 5 cm.
With 90° at both ends the arms are straight up from the base, side by side. They never meet.

Two angles that are each 90° or more always give arms that do not meet.

item.question: The angle at A is 40°. Find the smallest angle at B for which the arms from A and B do not meet, and say whether the length AB matters.
steps_tex: Draw $AB$ and the arm from $A$ at $40^\circ$. Call the line along this arm $l$.
The arm from $B$ that does not meet $l$ and leans the least is the line $m$ parallel to $l$.
$AB$ is a transversal of the parallel lines $l$ and $m$. The angles on the same side add to $180^\circ$.
So $\angle B = 180^\circ - 40^\circ = 140^\circ$.
Any $\angle B$ of $140^\circ$ or more does not meet $l$; any $\angle B$ less than $140^\circ$ does. The length of $AB$ is not used anywhere.
item.answer_tex: $\angle B = 140^\circ$: no triangle when $\angle B$ is $140^\circ$ or more; the length of $AB$ does not matter

item.question: Draw the altitude from A to the base BC of a triangle ABC using a ruler and a set square.
steps_tex: Keep the ruler along the base $BC$, and place the set square on the ruler with one edge of its right angle against the ruler.
Slide the set square along the ruler until its upright edge touches $A$.
Draw along the upright edge down from $A$ to $BC$. This segment $AD$ is the altitude.
$AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$, so the angle at $D$ is $90^\circ$, and the length of $AD$ is the height from $BC$ to $A$.
item.answer_tex: $AD$, the perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$, is the altitude from $A$; its length is the height

item.question: In a triangle ABC with a right angle at B, name two altitudes that are also sides.
steps_tex: $AB$ meets $BC$ at $90^\circ$. The perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ is $AB$ itself, so $AB$ is the altitude from $A$.
In the same way $BC$ meets $AB$ at $90^\circ$, so $BC$ is the altitude from $C$ to $AB$.
The altitude from $B$ goes to the long side $AC$ and lies inside the triangle.

item.question: Name the kind of triangle with sides (a) 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (b) 5 cm, 5 cm, 8 cm (c) 5 cm, 6 cm, 7 cm, after checking each really is a triangle.
steps: Check each with the triangle inequality: 5 < 5 + 5; 8 < 5 + 5; 7 < 5 + 6. All three exist.

(b) Exactly two sides are equal: isosceles.
(c) All three sides are different: scalene.

steps_tex: Every equilateral triangle has three equal angles, so each is $180^\circ \div 3 = 60^\circ$. No angle is $90^\circ$ or more.
So an equilateral triangle can be neither right-angled nor obtuse-angled.
Isosceles right-angled: take a right angle with two equal sides, for example $4\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$. The other two angles are equal and add up to $90^\circ$, so each is $45^\circ$.
Isosceles obtuse-angled: take an angle of $120^\circ$ between two equal sides of $5\text{ cm}$. The other two angles are equal and add up to $60^\circ$, so each is $30^\circ$.
item.answer_tex: (i) and (ii): not possible for an equilateral triangle; an isosceles triangle can be right-angled $(90^\circ$, $45^\circ$, $45^\circ)$ or obtuse-angled $(120^\circ$, $30^\circ$, $30^\circ)$

item.question: A spider walks from one corner of a box 6 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high to the opposite corner, over two faces. Which path is shortest?
steps: Lay two faces flat side by side. The path is a straight line across the joined faces.
Case 1: the line goes 6 cm along and 4 + 3 = 7 cm across. Draw this rectangle and measure the diagonal: about 9.2 cm.
Case 2: 4 cm along and 6 + 3 = 9 cm across. The diagonal measures about 9.8 cm.
Case 3: 3 cm along and 6 + 4 = 10 cm across. The diagonal measures about 10.4 cm.
The shortest is the first, about 9.2 cm. It is shorter than going along the edges, which is 6 + 4 + 3 = 13 cm.
